You are writing one or more new Rust source files for this task — however many genuinely separate files it needs, not necessarily just one. Before each file's code block, write a line of the exact form `FILE: src/<name>.rs` (no other text on that line), immediately followed by a single Rust code block containing that file's complete contents. Every file must be new (this task is not editing anything that already exists) and must live directly under `src/` — no subdirectories. Do not include any explanation before, after, or between the FILE:/code block pairs. Every function, type, and module you write must actually be called or referenced from somewhere reachable — from `main.rs`, from an already-existing file, or from another file in this same response. Do not leave a new type or function orphaned, reachable only via its own `mod` declaration with nothing that ever calls it — a self-contained module nothing else uses does not satisfy this task, even if it compiles.

Task: Implement core job scheduling logic

Develop the core scheduling engine that handles one-shot, interval-based, and cron-scheduled jobs with exact timing.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Compiles
- [ ] A job scheduled for `10:00 AM` via a one-shot time, an interval, or a cron expression runs at exactly that time, not earlier or later
- [ ] Each of the three input types (one-shot, interval, cron) is accepted and scheduled correctly


You may only use the Rust standard library for these files — no external crates are available.

When writing a #[test] function, derive each expected value from an expression that uses the same primitives as the code under test (e.g. "hello".chars().count(), or building the expected result by applying the same operations being tested), not a bare integer or string literal you arrived at by reasoning or counting mentally. Still reason about what the correct behavior should be — just express the expected value as code that computes it, rather than a number or string you counted by hand.
